summary: This document profiles the Certificate Management Protocol, the Certificate Request Message Format, and their HTTP or CoAP transfer for simple, interoperable, automated PKI operations. It is aimed at industrial and IoT use. Only the most important operations and options are kept, to make certificate management easy on constrained devices.

eli5.summary: A huge rulebook for getting ID cards was trimmed to the few pages small factory machines really need. That makes it quicker for them to get and renew their cards.

subtitle: A trimmed-down profile of CMP that lets industrial and IoT devices get and renew certificates automatically.

tldr.problem: CMP and CRMF offer a very large set of features and options, and many details are left open, so a full implementation is unrealistic for constrained devices and independent implementations may not interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The profile narrows CMP down to a few mandatory operations, such as initial enrollment and certificate update, specifies exhaustively how to build each message, and allows HTTP or CoAP transfer. Heavier logic is placed in the registration authorities rather than in the devices.
tldr.outcome: A conforming end entity only has to implement a small mandatory set, while more specialized needs such as central key generation, polling and batching stay available as optional features.

today: RFC 9483 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2023, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its algorithm guidance lives in RFC 9481.

sections.title: Why a Lightweight Profile
sections.content:
This document specifies PKI management operations for machine-to-machine and IoT use cases. Its focus is to maximize automation and interoperability between end entities (EEs), any number of intermediate registration authorities (RAs), and the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) endpoints of certification authority (CA) systems. It builds on CMP (RFC 4210, RFC 9480, RFC 9481), the Certificate Request Message Format (RFC 4211), CMS, HTTP transfer (RFC 6712) and CoAP transfer (RFC 9482).

CMP is capable, but it offers so many features and options that a full implementation is not realistic, and some details are not specified precisely. Profiling means keeping the strengths of the protocol while narrowing its options to those needed and removing ambiguity. The mandatory set is kept lean to limit development effort and resource needs on memory-constrained devices. Where complexity could sit either in the EE or in a PKI management entity, the profile puts it in the entity, which usually has more computing resources.

The RFC says it grew longer than the authors liked. Apart from Section 3, which has general requirements, readers need only the parts that match the operations and transfer they care about, guided by the conformance section.
sections.eli5: The big rulebook let machines do things in a hundred different ways. This paper picks a few simple ways, so small machines and big offices always understand each other.

sections.title: The PKI Architecture
sections.content:
A device hosting an EE is typically equipped with a manufacturer-issued device certificate, installed during production. It can protect the first enrollment of operational certificates, which are issued by the owner or operator and used in protocols like IPsec, TLS or SSH. In IEEE 802.1AR terms these are the IDevID and LDevID certificates. The owner using the manufacturer certificate MUST trust the manufacturer's trust anchor.

All operations follow the pull model. The EE (or an RA acting as an EE) creates a request, protects it, and sends it to a PKI management entity, which is an RA or a CA. An RA checks the request and either answers it or forwards it upstream. A typical chain is EE, local RA (LRA), RA, CA. Links between the entities may be synchronous, asynchronous, or even offline, such as file based.

The roles are: CA, which issues certificates; RA, to which a CA delegates functions such as authentication and authorization checks; LRA, an RA close to the end entities; and KGA, an optional key generation authority that offers key generation services to EEs.
sections.eli5: A machine asks a nearby clerk for an ID card. The clerk checks the request and either hands over the card or sends it up to the head office, which finally prints it.

sections.title: Common Message Rules and Error Handling
sections.content:
Every CMP message has a header, a body, optional protection and optional extraCerts. The profile fixes the general contents once, then each operation only describes its body.

  • Header: pvno MUST be 3 when EnvelopedData is expected or when hashAlg is used in certConf, and 2 otherwise. The transactionID in the first message MUST be 128 bits of random data, and later messages copy it. The senderNonce MUST be cryptographically secure and fresh 128 random bits. The recipNonce is absent in the first message and otherwise echoes the previous senderNonce.
  • Protection: signature-based protection is the default, and the same kind of protection MUST be used for every message of one operation. The protection covers header and body but not extraCerts.
  • extraCerts: with signature-based protection the first request and response carry the CMP protection certificate and its chain. Self-signed certificates should be omitted and MUST NOT be trusted merely because they were included.

On receipt, an entity checks ASN.1 syntax, pvno, transactionID, body type, nonces and protection. Messages without protection MUST be rejected except for some error messages.

Error handling is asymmetric. An EE SHALL NOT send error messages, and PKI management entities SHALL NOT send them upstream. An EE that rejects a new certificate without implicit confirmation reports it with a certConf carrying a rejection status. Entities report problems downstream with a rejection status or an error message, optionally with failInfo bits such as badPOP, badCertTemplate, notAuthorized or systemUnavail. An EE that gets systemUnavail or systemFailure should resend in a new transaction after some time.
sections.eli5: Every letter has the same envelope layout, a random ticket number, and a fresh secret code. A clerk checks all of that before reading further, and a letter without a proper seal gets thrown away.

sections.title: Enrollment, Revocation and Support Operations
sections.content:
Section 4 defines what an EE does with the PKI management entity it talks to.

  • New PKI (ir/ip): the EE authenticates with a certificate from an external PKI, such as a manufacturer device certificate. It sends one CertReqMsg, with certReqId 0, including a proof-of-possession signature over the certReq.
  • Known PKI (cr/cp): an additional certificate from a PKI the EE already has certificates from.
  • Update (kur/kup): renewing a still valid certificate, protected with the certificate to be updated. A new key pair should be used.
  • PKCS #10 (p10cr): a variant for CAs that do not support CRMF, with certReqId -1 in the response.
  • MAC-based enrollment: when the EE has no certificate but shares a secret with the entity. The secret is distributed out of band.

The EE includes the implicit confirmation request unless it requires certificate confirmation. If the entity grants it, no certConf/pkiConf round trip is needed. Otherwise the EE MUST send certConf, and a missing confirmation is handled like a rejection, after which the entity MAY revoke the certificate.

Central key generation is for EEs that cannot generate keys, for example for lack of entropy or computing power. The profile calls local generation strongly preferable. The KGA must hold a certificate with the id-kp-cmKGA extended key usage. The private key returns as an AsymmetricKeyPackage, signed in SignedData by the KGA and encrypted in EnvelopedData, using key transport, key agreement or a password-based technique depending on how the request was protected.

Revocation (rr/rp): signed with the certificate to be revoked. Support messages use genm/genp to get CA certificates, get a root CA certificate update (newWithNew, newWithOld and optional oldWithNew), get a certificate request template, or fetch a CRL update.

Delayed delivery: if a response is not ready, the entity answers with status waiting. The EE then sends pollReq, and pollRep carries a checkAfter value in seconds before the next poll, until the final response arrives.
sections.eli5: A machine can ask for a new card, ask for a swap before the old one runs out, or ask to cancel one. If the office is busy, it says "come back later" and the machine checks again after the time it was told.

sections.title: What RAs Do: Responding, Forwarding and Acting for Others
sections.content:
A PKI management entity that ends CMP MUST answer every request with a response or an error. It copies the request's sender into the response's recipient, copies the senderNonce into the recipNonce, and reuses the transactionID. It must also check that a new request does not reuse a transactionID already in use (transactionIdInUse).

An RA that forwards a message SHOULD NOT change it unless its role requires it, because changes imply reprotection, and that breaks end-to-end authentication or proof-of-possession. The profile gives these options:

  • Not changing protection: forward as a proxy. This variant, or adding protection, MUST be used for kur messages and for central key generation.
  • Adding protection: wrap the original request in a nested message signed by the RA. The original authentication stays intact and the RA signature shows it verified and approved the request.
  • Batching: bundle many messages in one nested message, typically between an LRA and an RA. Batch protection MUST NOT be read as approval of the bundled requests.
  • Replacing protection: for example swapping MAC-based protection for a signature that upstream entities can verify. If the RA changes the certTemplate, the original proof-of-possession breaks, so the RA verifies it and sets raVerified.

An RA may also act on behalf of an EE, requesting or revoking a certificate by signing with its own protection key. Upstream entities cannot tell this apart from replaced protection.
sections.eli5: A clerk in the middle can pass a form along untouched, staple a note saying "I checked this", or copy it to a new form with their own stamp. Changing the form means the original signature no longer counts, so the clerk must say they checked it.

sections.title: How Messages Travel
sections.content:
CMP messages are self-contained, so almost any reliable transfer can carry them. Entities SHOULD offer HTTP and MAY offer CoAP. Senders should use a configurable per-request timeout so a hanging transaction can be closed with an error (systemUnavail). Over HTTP, CoAP or MIME-based transfer the media type application/pkixcmp MUST be set.

HTTP and CoAP operations MUST use the URI path /.well-known/cmp or /.well-known/cmp/p/<name>, optionally followed by an operation label, such as initialization over HTTP or ir over CoAP. CMP already gives integrity, origin authentication and, for centrally generated keys, confidentiality end to end. TLS or DTLS can add hop-by-hop confidentiality as a second line of defense.

Other transfers: CMP may be piggybacked on other reliable protocols such as EAP or MQTT. For offline transfer, each file MUST hold exactly one DER-encoded CMP message with no extra header or trailer, and the file extension .pki MUST be used.
sections.eli5: The messages are sealed letters, so any reliable mail truck can carry them: web, a tiny-device protocol, or even a file on a USB stick with the name ending in .pki.

sections.title: What Implementations Must Support
sections.content:
The conformance section lists support for each operation by EE, RA and CA. The mandatory-to-implement set is deliberately limited, which is why the profile can still be called lightweight, particularly for end entities.

An EE MUST support enrolling to a new PKI (ir) and updating a valid certificate (kur). Enrolling to a known PKI, PKCS #10 enrollment, MAC-based enrollment, central key generation, support messages and polling are MAY for an EE, and revocation is SHOULD. CAs MUST support ir, kur, answering certificate requests and confirmations. RAs MUST support forwarding without changing protection and forwarding with added protection.

For message transfer, HTTP SHOULD be supported at all entities, while CoAP, piggybacking and offline transfer are MAY. The profile requires no specific transfer protocol, so devices with unusual constraints keep their freedom.
sections.eli5: The rules say which jobs every machine must be able to do and which are extras. A small machine only needs to know how to ask for a first card and how to renew it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of CMP, CMP Updates, CMP Algorithms, CRMF, the algorithm requirements update (RFC 9045), CMP over HTTP and CMP over CoAP all apply. The RFC adds guidance on trust anchors. All trust anchors MUST be stored on the device with integrity protection. A device short on storage may keep only a hash of each self-signed certificate and require the certificate in extraCerts, and any self-signed certificate provided in-band MUST be verified using information from the trust store.

When TLS uses shared-secret authentication, a pre-shared key (PSK) may be used with a secret of at least 128 bits of entropy, and otherwise a password-authenticated key exchange (PAKE) is recommended. Both resist real-time attacks equally, but only PAKE keeps long-term confidentiality independent of the secret's entropy. The RFC also stresses that the entropy of any shared secret sets the level of protection for MAC-based protection and for centrally generated keys.
sections.eli5: Keep the list of trusted offices safe from tampering, and if you use a password, make it long and random, because a short one is easy for a thief to guess.
